01_The_Solar_System_as_an_organised_syst.title: The Solar System as an organised system
01_The_Solar_System_as_an_organised_syst.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe the Sun, the eight planets in order, dwarf planets and asteroids, and moons, stating the correct orbital relationship between each category.

prerequisites.statement: A more massive object exerts a stronger gravitational pull, and gravity is the force that keeps one object orbiting another.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The whole Solar System hierarchy exists because the Sun's gravity, and then each planet's gravity, dominates the motion of the much less massive bodies around it.

prerequisites.statement: An orbit is a closed, repeating path that one body follows around another because of gravitational attraction.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Classifying a body correctly in this lesson always comes down to asking one question: what does it orbit?

diagnostic_items.question: The Sun's mass is about 330,000 times Earth's mass. Whose gravity dominates the Sun-Earth pair, and what does this produce?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The Sun's gravity dominates, because it is far more massive; this dominant pull is what bends Earth's path into a closed orbit around the Sun.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Earth's gravity dominates, because gravity is something planets have, not stars.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats gravity as a property only of 'planet-like' objects rather than as something every mass has, with strength depending on mass.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Neither dominates, they pull on each other equally so neither one moves.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner correctly recalls that the forces are equal and opposite, but wrongly concludes this means neither object's motion is affected; the much less massive body is the one whose path visibly bends.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner can identify which body's gravity dominates a pair before using that idea to justify the whole Solar System's orbital structure.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Compare the two masses directly and state out loud which object is 'massive enough to barely move' and which is 'light enough to be swung into a path' before describing the orbit.

theory_blocks.title: One gravity, one organised family
theory_blocks.body:
The Solar System is not a random scatter of objects: it is organised, and gravity is what does the organising.

The Solar System has just **one star, the Sun**, and it holds about [[blue:99.8%]] of all the mass in the Solar System, so its gravitational pull dominates everything near it.

Every planet, dwarf planet and asteroid is continually falling toward the Sun under this pull, but each one also has sideways motion, so instead of falling in, it sweeps around the Sun in a closed path: an **orbit**.

The same idea repeats on a smaller scale. A planet's own gravity can be strong enough to hold smaller bodies, called **moons**, in orbit around itself, even while the planet is itself orbiting the Sun.

The result is a nested structure: moons orbit planets, planets (and smaller bodies) orbit the Sun, and the whole system is held together by one force acting at every level.

theory_blocks.title: The eight planets, in order from the Sun
theory_blocks.body:
A **planet** is a body that orbits the Sun directly and is large enough for its own gravity to have pulled it into a (nearly) round shape. In order of increasing distance from the Sun, the eight planets are:

Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the four smaller, rocky inner planets. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are the four much larger outer planets, made mostly of gas and ice.

This order is fixed: it is set by each planet's orbital distance from the Sun, not by size, mass or anything else.

theory_blocks.title: Asteroids, dwarf planets, and why Pluto was reclassified
theory_blocks.body:
Cambridge groups dwarf planets and asteroids together as **minor planets**: bodies that orbit the Sun directly but are not classed as planets.

**Asteroids** are rocky bodies, much smaller than planets, that orbit the Sun directly; most lie in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

A **dwarf planet** also orbits the Sun directly and is round, but fails a third test that a planet must pass: it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other similarly sized bodies.

Pluto shares its region of space (the Kuiper belt) with many other icy bodies of comparable size, so since 2006 it has been classified as a dwarf planet rather than a planet, even though it is round and orbits the Sun directly.

So the full test for 'planet' has three parts: (1) orbits the Sun directly; (2) is massive enough to be round; (3) has cleared its orbital neighbourhood.

Pluto passes (1) and (2) but fails (3), which is exactly why the earlier 'nine planets' list changed to eight.

theory_blocks.title: A moon orbits its planet, not the Sun directly
theory_blocks.body:
A **moon** is a body that orbits a planet, not the Sun directly. This does not contradict the Sun's overall dominance: the Earth-Moon pair, as a whole, still orbits the Sun once a year, while at the same time the Moon orbits Earth once a month.

Both statements are true together, at two different levels of the same nested structure.

The test for 'what does this object orbit?' always has one correct, single answer at the level you are asking about: [[blue:the Moon's immediate orbit is around Earth;

Earth's immediate orbit is around the Sun.]] Never collapse the two levels into one sentence like 'the Moon orbits the Sun', even though, zoomed far enough out, it is carried around the Sun along with Earth.

keywords.definition: A closed, repeating path that one body follows around another because of gravitational attraction.
A body that orbits the Sun directly, is massive enough for its own gravity to make it round, and has cleared its orbital neighbourhood of similarly sized bodies.
A body that orbits the Sun directly and is round, but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of similarly sized bodies.
A rocky body that orbits the Sun directly but is not massive enough to be round.
A body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun directly.

worked_examples.statement: **Putting planets in order.** Arrange these four planets in order of increasing distance from the Sun: Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus.
knowns: The fixed order of all eight planets is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
unknowns: The order of just these four planets.
reasoning: Locate each of the four named planets within the full fixed order.
Keep only those four, preserving their relative order from the full list.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check against the full list: Mercury (1st), Venus (2nd), Mars (4th), Jupiter (5th) — their relative order (1,2,4,5) is already increasing, so no swap is needed.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Ordering by size or by how familiar the name sounds, rather than by the fixed distance order from the Sun.

worked_examples.statement: **Classifying four bodies.** Classify each of the following as a planet, a dwarf planet, an asteroid, or a moon: (a) Saturn, (b) Titan (which orbits Saturn), (c) Ceres (which orbits the Sun directly, in the asteroid belt, and is round), (d) a 2 km rock in the asteroid belt that orbits the Sun directly and is irregular in shape.
knowns: Planet: orbits the Sun directly, round, has cleared its neighbourhood.
Dwarf planet: orbits the Sun directly, round, has NOT cleared its neighbourhood.
Asteroid: orbits the Sun directly, not round.
Moon: orbits a planet, not the Sun directly.
unknowns: The classification of each of the four named bodies.
reasoning: For each body, first ask what it orbits directly.
If it orbits the Sun directly, then ask whether it is round; if round, it is either a planet or a dwarf planet depending on whether it has cleared its neighbourhood.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) Saturn is a planet (orbits the Sun directly, round, has cleared its orbital neighbourhood). (b) Titan is a moon (orbits Saturn, not the Sun directly).

(c) Ceres is a dwarf planet (orbits the Sun directly, round, has not cleared other bodies from its orbital neighbourhood). (d) The 2 km rock is an asteroid (orbits the Sun directly, not round).
worked_examples.interpretation: Every classification used the same three-question test consistently, which is why Ceres and the small rock get different answers even though both are in the asteroid belt.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Classifying Ceres as 'just an asteroid' because it lies in the asteroid belt, instead of checking that it is round and so meets the dwarf-planet criterion.

worked_examples.statement: **Why isn't Pluto a planet?** Explain, using the three-part test for a planet, why Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet rather than a planet.
knowns: Pluto orbits the Sun directly.
Pluto is round (massive enough for its own gravity to pull it into a near-spherical shape).
Pluto shares the Kuiper belt with many other icy bodies of comparable size.
unknowns: Which of the three planet criteria Pluto fails.
reasoning: Check criterion 1 (orbits the Sun directly): satisfied.
Check criterion 2 (round): satisfied.
Check criterion 3 (cleared its orbital neighbourhood): this is the one that fails, because Pluto shares its region of space with many similarly sized Kuiper-belt bodies.
worked_examples.solution:
Pluto passes the first two tests (it orbits the Sun directly and is round) but fails the third: it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other similarly sized bodies.

Failing even one of the three criteria is enough to place it in the dwarf-planet category instead of the planet category.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is exactly why the classification changed in 2006 without Pluto itself changing at all: the definition of 'planet' was made precise, and Pluto was re-sorted under the new, clearer test.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying Pluto 'is too small' to be a planet, when size alone is not the criterion that excludes it; several moons are larger than Pluto. The excluding criterion is specifically about clearing its orbital neighbourhood.

guided_exercises.statement: Put these five planets in order of increasing distance from the Sun: Neptune, Earth, Uranus, Mercury, Saturn.
hints: Write out the full fixed order of all eight planets first, from memory.
Cross out the three planets not named in this question.
Read off the remaining five in the order they appear in your full list.
common_errors: Placing Saturn after Uranus, confusing the two outer gas giants' order.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Write out the full fixed order of all eight planets first, from memory.

**Step 2 — Method:** Cross out the three planets not named in this question.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Mercury, Earth, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

**Step 4 — Check:** Read off the remaining five in the order they appear in your full list.

guided_exercises.statement: Classify each body: (a) Europa, which orbits Jupiter; (b) Makemake, which orbits the Sun directly, is round, and shares the Kuiper belt with many similar bodies; (c) Mars, which orbits the Sun directly, is round, and has cleared its orbital neighbourhood.
hints: Ask first: does this body orbit the Sun directly, or a planet?
If it orbits the Sun directly and is round, ask whether it has cleared its orbital neighbourhood.
A 'yes' to clearing its neighbourhood gives a planet; a 'no' gives a dwarf planet.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) Europa is a moon (orbits Jupiter, not the Sun directly). (b) Makemake is a dwarf planet (orbits the Sun directly, round, has not cleared its neighbourhood). (c) Mars is a planet (orbits the Sun directly, round, has cleared its neighbourhood).
common_errors: Calling Europa a 'small planet' because it is round and orbits something, without checking what it orbits.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Ask first: does this body orbit the Sun directly, or a planet?

**Step 2 — Method:** If it orbits the Sun directly and is round, ask whether it has cleared its orbital neighbourhood.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** (a) Europa is a moon (orbits Jupiter, not the Sun directly). (b) Makemake is a dwarf planet (orbits the Sun directly, round, has not cleared its neighbourhood). (c) Mars is a planet (orbits the Sun directly, round, has cleared its neighbourhood).

**Step 4 — Check:** A 'yes' to clearing its neighbourhood gives a planet; a 'no' gives a dwarf planet.

exercises.statement: Write out all eight planets in order of increasing distance from the Sun.
exercises.answer: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
exercises.full_solution: This is the fixed order; no calculation is involved, only correct recall of the orbital sequence.

exercises.statement: Classify each body as a planet, a dwarf planet, an asteroid, or a moon: (a) Phobos, which orbits Mars; (b) Eris, which orbits the Sun directly, is round, and shares its region of space with similar bodies; (c) an irregular 500 m rock that orbits the Sun directly in the asteroid belt.
exercises.answer: (a) Phobos is a moon. (b) Eris is a dwarf planet. (c) The 500 m rock is an asteroid.
exercises.full_solution: Phobos orbits a planet (Mars), not the Sun, so it is a moon. Eris orbits the Sun directly and is round, but has not cleared its neighbourhood, so it is a dwarf planet. The 500 m rock orbits the Sun directly but is not round, so it is an asteroid.

exercises.statement: A classmate says: 'The Moon orbits the Sun, just like every other object in the Solar System.' Give the correct, more precise statement, and explain what is missing from the classmate's sentence.
exercises.answer: The Moon orbits Earth directly; the Earth-Moon pair, together, orbits the Sun. The classmate's sentence skips the intermediate step and states only the outermost level of the nested structure.
exercises.full_solution: Both 'the Moon orbits Earth' and 'the Earth-Moon pair orbits the Sun' are true at the same time, but they describe two different levels of the Solar System's nested orbital structure, and only the first one answers the question 'what does the Moon orbit directly?'.

exercises.statement: Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance of about 1 Astronomical Unit (AU). Jupiter orbits at about 5.2 AU and Neptune at about 30.1 AU. If a scale model represents Earth's orbit as a circle of radius 10 cm, calculate the radius that would represent (a) Jupiter's orbit and (b) Neptune's orbit in the same model.
exercises.answer: (a) Jupiter's model radius $=5.2\times10\,\mathrm{cm}=52\,\mathrm{cm}$. (b) Neptune's model radius $=30.1\times10\,\mathrm{cm}=301\,\mathrm{cm}$ (about 3.0 m).
exercises.full_solution: The model scales every real distance by the same factor: $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ represents $1\,\mathrm{AU}$, so any distance in AU is multiplied by $10\,\mathrm{cm}$. For Jupiter: $5.2\times10=52$. For Neptune: $30.1\times10=301$. This is exactly why a single diagram cannot show both the correct orbital order and a true distance scale on an ordinary page: Neptune's model orbit would need to be about 30 times wider than Earth's.

exam_questions.statement: (a) State which single body all eight planets orbit directly. [1] (b) Name the two planets that are immediate neighbours of Earth in the fixed orbital order, stating which is closer to the Sun and which is farther. [2] (c) Ceres orbits the Sun directly and is round, but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of similar-sized bodies. State its classification. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) The Sun. (b) Venus is the neighbour closer to the Sun than Earth; Mars is the neighbour farther from the Sun than Earth. (c) Ceres is a dwarf planet.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The Sun. (b) Venus is the neighbour closer to the Sun than Earth; Mars is the neighbour farther from the Sun than Earth. (c) Ceres is a dwarf planet.
mark_scheme: States the Sun. [1]
Names Venus as closer to the Sun than Earth. [1]
Names Mars as farther from the Sun than Earth. [1]
States 'dwarf planet' for Ceres. [1]
common_errors: Naming Mercury instead of Venus as Earth's inner neighbour, skipping a step in the order.

exam_questions.statement: A student claims Pluto should still be called the ninth planet because 'it orbits the Sun and is round, just like the other planets.' (a) State the two planet criteria that the student has correctly identified Pluto as satisfying. [2] (b) State the criterion the student has missed, and explain, using this missing criterion, why Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet. [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a) The student has correctly identified that Pluto orbits the Sun directly and is round (massive enough for its own gravity to make it near-spherical). (b) The missing criterion is clearing its orbital neighbourhood of other similarly sized bodies. Pluto shares the Kuiper belt with many icy bodies of comparable size, so it fails this third criterion, which is why it is classified as a dwarf planet rather than a planet.
exam_questions.full_solution: A full planet must pass all three criteria; passing two out of three is not enough. Pluto's case shows that 'round' and 'orbits the Sun directly' do not by themselves make something a planet.
mark_scheme: States that Pluto orbits the Sun directly. [1]
States that Pluto is round. [1]
Identifies 'clearing its orbital neighbourhood' as the missing criterion. [1]
States that Pluto shares the Kuiper belt with similarly sized bodies. [1]
Concludes correctly that this is why Pluto is a dwarf planet, not a planet. [1]
common_errors: Explaining the reclassification purely in terms of Pluto's small size, which is not the criterion actually being tested.

mcq.stem: Which of the following lists four planets in the correct order of increasing distance from the Sun?

options.text: Earth, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter
options.why_wrong: places Earth before Mercury, but Mercury is closer to the Sun than Earth.

options.text: Mercury, Earth, Mars, Jupiter
Mercury, Mars, Earth, Jupiter
options.why_wrong: swaps Earth and Mars; Earth is closer to the Sun than Mars.

options.text: Jupiter, Mars, Earth, Mercury
options.why_wrong: lists the four planets in decreasing distance from the Sun, the reverse of what was asked.

mcq.explanation: The fixed order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter...; keeping only these four in that order gives Mercury, Earth, Mars, Jupiter.

mcq.stem: Why is Pluto classified as a dwarf planet rather than one of the eight planets?

options.text: It does not orbit the Sun.
options.why_wrong: is false; Pluto does orbit the Sun directly, so this cannot be the reason for its reclassification.

options.text: It is not round.
options.why_wrong: is false; Pluto is massive enough for its own gravity to make it round, like the eight planets.

options.text: It has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other similarly sized bodies.
It is too far from the Sun to be seen clearly.
options.why_wrong: confuses observational difficulty with the actual classification criterion, which has nothing to do with how easily an object can be observed.

mcq.explanation: Pluto passes the 'orbits the Sun' and 'round' tests but fails the third: it shares the Kuiper belt with many similarly sized bodies, so it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly describes the Moon's orbit?

options.text: The Moon orbits the Sun directly, the same as any planet.
options.why_wrong: skips the intermediate level: the Moon's immediate orbit is around Earth, not directly around the Sun.

options.text: The Moon does not orbit anything; it simply follows Earth around.
options.why_wrong: denies that the Moon is in orbit at all, when it is held in a genuine closed orbit around Earth by Earth's gravity.

options.text: The Moon orbits the Sun, and Earth orbits the Moon.
options.why_wrong: reverses the Earth-Moon relationship; Earth is far more massive, so the Moon orbits Earth, not the other way around.

options.text: The Moon orbits Earth, and the Earth-Moon pair together orbits the Sun.

mcq.explanation: The Moon's immediate orbit is around Earth; at the larger scale, the Earth-Moon pair together orbits the Sun. Both statements hold at the same time, at two different levels.

mcq.stem: A newly found rocky body orbits the Sun directly, lies in the asteroid belt, and has an irregular, non-round shape. How should it be classified?

options.text: As an asteroid.
As a planet.
options.why_wrong: requires the body to be round as well as orbiting the Sun directly; this body is not round.

options.text: As a dwarf planet.
options.why_wrong: requires the body to be round; a dwarf planet still has to pass the 'round' test, just not the 'cleared its neighbourhood' test.

options.text: As a moon.
options.why_wrong: requires the body to orbit a planet; this body orbits the Sun directly, not a planet.

mcq.explanation: It orbits the Sun directly but is not round, which is exactly the asteroid case, distinct from both the planet and dwarf-planet categories (which both require roundness).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Pluto is one of the eight planets of the Solar System.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Older textbooks, posters and popular culture still list Pluto among 'the nine planets', a classification used before 2006.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner includes Pluto when reciting or writing out the eight-planet order.
misconceptions.correct_model: Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets. The eight planets run from Mercury to Neptune.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the learner state the eight-planet order first with no extra names, then separately place Pluto in the dwarf-planet category and give the classification reason (it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of similarly sized debris).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A moon orbits the Sun directly, in the same way a planet does.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In the big picture everything in the Solar System does eventually travel around the Sun, so it is easy to skip the intermediate step and describe a moon's path as 'around the Sun'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes the Moon's motion without mentioning Earth at all.
misconceptions.correct_model: A moon orbits its planet; the planet and its moon then travel together around the Sun. Both statements are true at the same time.
misconceptions.remediation: Use the Earth-Moon-Sun case explicitly: the Moon orbits Earth, and the Earth-Moon pair together orbits the Sun, and ask the learner to say both sentences out loud, in that order.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Every object in the Solar System is a planet.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 'Planet' is used loosely in everyday speech for almost anything large orbiting the Sun.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner calls an asteroid, a dwarf planet or a moon 'a planet'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Only eight bodies are classified as planets. Asteroids, dwarf planets and moons are separate categories, each with its own defining criterion, even though all of them are part of the Solar System.
misconceptions.remediation: Before naming any object, ask the three sorting questions in order: does it orbit the Sun directly, or a planet? Is it large enough and round enough, and has it cleared its orbital neighbourhood?

common_mistakes.mistake: Including Pluto when reciting the eight planets.
common_mistakes.why: Older sources and everyday culture still describe 'nine planets'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State the eight-planet order with no extra names, then separately classify Pluto using the three-part test.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing the Moon's orbit as being directly around the Sun.
common_mistakes.why: In the very big picture everything does end up moving around the Sun, so the intermediate step is easy to skip.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always answer 'what does this body orbit directly?' at exactly one level at a time: the Moon orbits Earth; Earth orbits the Sun.

common_mistakes.mistake: Classifying Ceres or another round body in the asteroid belt simply as 'an asteroid' because of its location.
common_mistakes.why: Location is being used instead of the actual classification criteria.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check roundness and whether the orbital neighbourhood has been cleared before classifying any body, regardless of where it is found.

exam_notes: When asked to classify a body, always run through the full three-question test (orbits what? round? neighbourhood cleared?) rather than guessing from the body's name or location.
State orbital relationships at one level at a time: 'X orbits Y' should name a single, immediate body, not skip a level.
Pluto's reclassification should be explained using the specific missing criterion (clearing its orbital neighbourhood), not vague statements about its size.

summary.big_idea: Gravity organises the Solar System into a nested structure: moons orbit planets, planets and smaller bodies orbit the Sun, and every category (planet, dwarf planet, asteroid, moon) is defined by what it orbits and whether it is round.
key_points: The eight planets, in fixed order from the Sun, are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
A planet must orbit the Sun directly, be round, and have cleared its orbital neighbourhood; failing any one of these gives a different classification.
Pluto orbits the Sun directly and is round but has not cleared its neighbourhood, so it is a dwarf planet, not a planet.
A moon orbits a planet, not the Sun directly, even though the planet-moon pair together still orbits the Sun.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Before naming any Solar System body, ask what it orbits directly, whether it is round, and whether it has cleared its orbital neighbourhood: those three questions sort every case in this lesson correctly.

objectives.statement: Define the light-year as a distance, calculate the time light takes to travel a given distance, state that the Sun is the closest star and a medium-sized star made mostly of hydrogen and helium, explain that the Sun's mass and gravity dominate the Solar System, and state that it radiates most of its energy as infrared, visible and ultraviolet radiation.

Use orbital speed $v=2\pi r/T$ for a circular orbit, explain why orbital speed and gravitational field strength both decrease for planets farther from the Sun, and explain that stable stars release energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.

prerequisites.statement: Speed is distance travelled divided by time taken, $v=d/t$, and this relationship can be rearranged for any of the three quantities.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both the light-travel-time calculation and the orbital-speed calculation in this lesson are rearrangements of exactly this one relationship.

prerequisites.statement: The circumference of a circle of radius $r$ is $2\pi r$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A circular orbit's path length in one period is its circumference, which is the distance used in the orbital-speed calculation.

prerequisites.statement: A more massive object exerts a stronger gravitational pull on a given body at a given distance.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The Sun's gravity dominates the Solar System precisely because it holds almost all of the system's mass.

diagnostic_items.question: A probe travels $6.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}$ at a steady speed of $3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Rearrange $v=d/t$ and find the time taken.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner recognises the two quantities but combines them by multiplying instead of rearranging $v=d/t$ correctly; a quick unit check (m × m/s) shows the answer cannot be a time.
The learner has the fraction upside down, dividing speed by distance; the absurdly small answer for an enormous distance is the signal.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks that the learner can rearrange $v=d/t$ into $t=d/v$ and divide numbers in standard form, which is exactly the step used later for light-travel time and for orbital speed.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Rearrange $v=d/t$ on paper before substituting any numbers, then divide the decimal parts and subtract the powers of ten as two separate steps, and finish with a unit check.

diagnostic_items.question: A circle has radius $r=5.0\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}$. How far is it all the way round the circle?

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has used the area formula instead of the circumference; the squared metres give it away, since a distance round a path must be in metres.
The learner has dropped the factor of 2, giving half the circumference; this would later halve every orbital speed calculated from $v=2\pi r/T$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks that the learner can produce the circumference $2\pi r$ of a circle of given radius, which is the distance travelled in one orbit and therefore the numerator of $v=2\pi r/T$.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write the two circle formulas side by side, $C=2\pi r$ (a length, in metres) and $A=\pi r^{2}$ (an area, in square metres), and pick the one whose unit matches a distance travelled.

theory_blocks.title: Light as a ruler for enormous distances
theory_blocks.body:
Space distances are so large that an ordinary unit like the kilometre becomes awkward to write and to picture.

Light offers a natural alternative: it travels through vacuum at a fixed, enormous speed, $c=3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the distance light covers in a fixed time is itself a convenient, fixed distance.

A [[blue:**light-year**]] is defined as the distance light travels through vacuum in one year. It is a unit of **distance**, even though its name is built from a time.

The Sun is the **closest star to Earth** (its light takes about 8 minutes to reach us); the next nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

Saying 'that star is 4 light-years away' means exactly the same kind of statement as 'that town is 60 miles away': both name a length, not a duration.

theory_blocks.title: From distance and speed to travel time
theory_blocks.body:
Light travel time is found with the same relationship used for any constant speed: $v=d/t$, rearranged to $t=d/v$. For light, $v=c=3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the travel time for a given distance $d$ is $t=d/c$.

For example, the Sun is about $d=1.5\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$ from Earth. The travel time is $t=\dfrac{1.5\times10^{11}}{3.0\times10^{8}}=500\,\mathrm{s}\approx8.3\,\mathrm{min}$.

Check by substituting back: $500\,\mathrm{s}\times3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}=1.5\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, which recovers the original distance, confirming the calculation.

theory_blocks.title: Gravity bends a path into an orbit
theory_blocks.body:
The Sun is a **medium-sized star**, made mostly of hydrogen and helium, and it contains about 99.8% of the Solar System's total mass.

Its gravitational pull on each planet is therefore far stronger than the pull between any two planets.

(By Newton's third law the planet pulls back on the Sun with an equal force, but the Sun is so massive that this barely moves it, while the planet's much smaller mass lets its path be bent into an orbit.)

The Sun's pull on a planet always points from the planet toward the Sun.

A force directed toward a fixed centre, while the object is already moving sideways, does not speed the object up or slow it down along its path; it continuously changes the object's **direction**.

Applied every instant, this continuous bending turns what would otherwise be a straight-line path into a closed, repeating curve: an orbit.

No separate forward force is needed to 'keep the planet going' along the orbit; a planet's sideways motion, once established, continues on its own, and gravity's entire job is to keep redirecting it toward the Sun.

assets.caption: A circular orbit of radius $r$ (green dashed line). The short red arrow $F$ is the Sun's gravitational pull on the planet: it points from the planet toward the Sun, perpendicular to the planet's velocity $v$, so it changes the planet's direction and not its speed. One full trip around the circumference $2\pi r$ takes one period $T$, giving $v=2\pi r/T$.
assets.purpose: Make explicit that the gravitational force is centripetal (toward the centre), not tangential, and separate the distance quantity ($r$, $2\pi r$) from the time quantity ($T$).

theory_blocks.title: What the Sun radiates
theory_blocks.body:
Gravity is how the Sun governs the planets' motion; **radiation** is how it reaches them with energy.

That energy leaves the Sun as electromagnetic radiation travelling outwards in all directions, and the Sun radiates [[blue:most of its energy in the infrared, visible and ultraviolet regions]] of the electromagnetic spectrum.

This is why the Sun both lights and warms the Solar System: its visible radiation is what we see by, its infrared radiation is absorbed by surfaces and raises their temperature, and its ultraviolet radiation is the part that burns skin.

The energy the Sun radiates is released by nuclear fusion deep in its core, a nuclear process and not ordinary burning; the detail of that process is Supplement content, set out in 'A stable star shines by fusing hydrogen into helium'.

theory_blocks.title: Orbital speed for a circular orbit
theory_blocks.body:
For a circular orbit, the planet travels the full circumference, $2\pi r$, once every orbital period, $T$.

Since speed is distance divided by time, the orbital speed is $$v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}.$$ Here $r$ is a distance (metres) and $T$ is a time (seconds);

keep the two units clearly separate, since $r$ and $T$ for a given planet come from completely different kinds of measurement (how far away it is, and how long it takes to go around once).

This simplified circular model is good enough at this level for every planet in the Solar System; real orbits are slightly elliptical, which is a refinement beyond this course.

theory_blocks.title: Farther from the Sun means weaker pull and slower orbit
theory_blocks.body:
The Sun's gravitational field strength falls off with distance: it is much weaker at Neptune's orbit than at Mercury's.

One consequence is that a planet farther from the Sun also needs a lower orbital speed to stay in a stable circular orbit; weaker gravity bends the path more gently, and a more gently bending path matches a slower-moving object.

This trend is confirmed by the orbital-speed formula applied to real planets: Mercury (closest, $r\approx5.8\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}$, $T\approx88$ days) orbits at about $48\,\mathrm{km/s}$;

Earth ($r\approx1.5\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, $T=365.25$ days) orbits at about $30\,\mathrm{km/s}$; Mars ($r\approx2.28\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, $T\approx687$ days) orbits at about $24\,\mathrm{km/s}$.

Orbital speed drops steadily as $r$ increases, exactly as the weakening pull of gravity predicts.

theory_blocks.title: A stable star shines by fusing hydrogen into helium
theory_blocks.body:
A stable star such as the Sun releases its energy by **nuclear fusion**: in its extremely hot, high-pressure core, hydrogen nuclei join together to form helium nuclei, releasing energy in the process.

This is a nuclear process, completely different from ordinary chemical burning (combustion), which only rearranges electrons between atoms and requires oxygen. Fusion needs no oxygen at all;

it needs extreme temperature and pressure, found naturally only deep inside a star.

This steady release of energy in the core is the ultimate source of everything the Sun radiates into space, and it is what lets a stable star go on shining steadily for billions of years.

keywords.definition: The distance light travels through vacuum in one year; a unit of distance.
The time taken for an orbiting body to complete one full orbit.
For a circular orbit, the orbit's circumference divided by its period, $v=2\pi r/T$.
A force directed toward the centre of a circular path, which changes an object's direction without changing its speed.
A nuclear process in which light nuclei join together to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy; it powers the Sun and other stable stars.

worked_examples.statement: **Sunlight's travel time.** Light travels at $c=3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The Sun is about $1.5\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$ from Earth. Calculate how long sunlight takes to reach Earth, in seconds and in minutes.
knowns: $d=1.5\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$
$c=3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$
reasoning: Rearrange $v=d/t$ to $t=d/v$, using $c$ in place of $v$.
Substitute the given values and divide.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Multiplying distance by speed instead of dividing, which gives a nonsensical result with the wrong units.

worked_examples.statement: **Light from Neptune.** Neptune orbits at about $4.5\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ from the Sun. Calculate how long sunlight takes to reach Neptune, giving your answer in minutes.
knowns: $d=4.5\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$
$c=3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$
reasoning: Use $t=d/c$ exactly as before.
Convert the result from seconds to minutes by dividing by 60.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $15{,}000\,\mathrm{s}\times3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}=4.5\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$, matching the given distance. This is about 30 times Earth's own 500 s delay, consistent with Neptune being about 30 times farther from the Sun.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Leaving the answer in seconds when the question specifically asks for minutes, or dividing by 60 twice by mistake.

worked_examples.statement: **Earth's orbital speed.** Earth orbits the Sun at an average radius $r=1.5\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, completing one orbit in $T=365.25$ days. Calculate Earth's orbital speed in $\mathrm{m/s}$, given $1$ day $=86\,400\,\mathrm{s}$.
knowns: $r=1.5\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$
reasoning: Use $v=2\pi r/T$.
Convert $T$ into seconds before substituting, since $r$ is already in metres.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by substitution: $v\times T=2.99\times10^{4}\times3.156\times10^{7}\approx9.4\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, which matches the orbit's circumference $2\pi r=9.4\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Substituting $T$ in days directly without converting to seconds, which gives a speed about 86,400 times too large.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing two planets.** Mars orbits at $r=2.28\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$ with period $T=687$ days. (a) Calculate Mars's orbital speed in $\mathrm{m/s}$. (b) State and explain, without recalculating, whether you expect this speed to be larger or smaller than Earth's orbital speed of about $3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
unknowns: Mars's orbital speed $v$; comparison with Earth
reasoning: Convert $T$ to seconds, then apply $v=2\pi r/T$.
For part (b), use the rule that gravitational pull, and hence orbital speed, decreases with distance from the Sun.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) $v=\dfrac{2\pi\times2.28\times10^{11}}{5.936\times10^{7}}\approx2.41\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}\approx24\,\mathrm{km/s}$.

(b) This is smaller than Earth's $30\,\mathrm{km/s}$, as expected, because Mars is farther from the Sun, so the Sun's gravitational pull on it is weaker and a lower orbital speed is enough to maintain a stable circular orbit.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming a larger orbital radius must give a larger speed, by analogy with 'farther means faster' from unrelated everyday contexts, instead of applying the actual trend of weakening gravity with distance.

guided_exercises.statement: A distant object is $9.0\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ from Earth. Calculate how long light takes to travel this distance, in seconds and then in minutes.
hints: Identify which relationship connects distance, speed and time.
Rearrange it to make time the subject before substituting any numbers.
Convert your final answer in seconds into minutes by dividing by 60.
common_errors: Forgetting to convert the final answer from seconds to minutes when the question asks for both.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify which relationship connects distance, speed and time.

**Step 2 — Method:** Rearrange it to make time the subject before substituting any numbers.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $t=\dfrac{9.0\times10^{12}}{3.0\times10^{8}}=3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{s}=500\,\mathrm{min}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Convert your final answer in seconds into minutes by dividing by 60.

guided_exercises.statement: Mercury orbits the Sun at $r=5.8\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}$ with a period of $T=88$ days. Calculate Mercury's orbital speed in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
hints: Convert the period from days to seconds first ($1$ day $=86\,400\,\mathrm{s}$).
Use $v=2\pi r/T$ with $r$ in metres and $T$ in seconds.
Check your answer is larger than Earth's $3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, since Mercury is closer to the Sun.
common_errors: Using the period in days without converting to seconds, giving a wildly oversized answer.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Convert the period from days to seconds first ($1$ day $=86\,400\,\mathrm{s}$).

**Step 2 — Method:** Use $v=2\pi r/T$ with $r$ in metres and $T$ in seconds.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $T=88\times86\,400=7.60\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{s}$; $v=\dfrac{2\pi\times5.8\times10^{10}}{7.60\times10^{6}}\approx4.8\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}\approx48\,\mathrm{km/s}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer is larger than Earth's $3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, since Mercury is closer to the Sun.

exercises.statement: A student writes: 'Proxima Centauri is 4.2 light-years away, so it took 4.2 light-years for its light to reach us.' Identify and correct the error in this sentence.
exercises.answer: The error treats 'light-year' as a unit of time. The corrected sentence is: 'Proxima Centauri is 4.2 light-years away, so its light took 4.2 years to reach us.'
exercises.full_solution: A light-year is a distance (the distance light travels in one year); the corresponding travel time for that same distance is 1 year for every light-year of distance, which is why 4.2 light-years of distance corresponds to 4.2 years of travel time, not 4.2 light-years of time.

exercises.statement: Venus orbits the Sun at about $1.08\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$. Calculate the time sunlight takes to reach Venus, in seconds.

Jupiter orbits at $r=7.80\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$ with a period of $T=11.86$ years ($1$ year $=3.156\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}$). Calculate Jupiter's orbital speed in $\mathrm{m/s}$, and state whether it is larger or smaller than Earth's $3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $v\times T\approx1.31\times10^{4}\times3.74\times10^{8}\approx4.90\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$, matching $2\pi r\approx4.90\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$. The result is smaller than Earth's speed, consistent with Jupiter being much farther from the Sun.

exercises.statement: A spacecraft engineer says: 'Our probe keeps slowing down in its orbit, so its engine must have failed and it needs a boost to keep orbiting.' Using the idea of gravity as a centripetal force, explain what is actually wrong with assuming a stable circular orbit requires an ongoing engine boost.
exercises.answer: A stable circular orbit does not need an ongoing forward boost at all: gravity continuously redirects the probe toward the central body without speeding it up or slowing it down, so a probe in a genuinely stable circular orbit keeps a constant speed without any engine firing.
exercises.full_solution: If the probe really is slowing down, the orbit is not behaving as a stable circular orbit (perhaps it is elliptical, or atmospheric drag is acting), but the general claim that 'orbits need a continuous engine boost to keep going' is itself the misconception: gravity alone, acting toward the centre, is what sustains a stable circular orbit indefinitely.

exam_questions.statement: Light from a star takes $6.4$ years to reach Earth. (a) State how far away the star is, in light-years. [1] (b) The speed of light is $c=3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $1$ year $=3.156\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the star's distance from Earth in metres. [3] (c) Explain why 'light-year' is a unit of distance rather than a unit of time. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $6.4$ light-years. (b) distance $=c\times t=3.0\times10^{8}\times(6.4\times3.156\times10^{7})\approx6.06\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}$. (c) A light-year names the distance light covers in one year of travel at a fixed speed, so it measures a length, not a duration, even though a time (one year) is used to define it.
mark_scheme: States 6.4 light-years. [1]
Converts 6.4 years into seconds correctly. [1]
Multiplies by the speed of light to get a distance in metres. [1]
Reaches a value of approximately $6.1\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}$ (accept $5.8$-$6.2\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}$). [1]
Explains that a light-year names a distance because it is 'speed multiplied by a fixed time', giving a length. [1]
common_errors: Leaving the distance in years rather than converting to metres when the question explicitly asks for metres.

exam_questions.statement: Saturn orbits the Sun at $r=1.43\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ with a period $T=29.5$ years ($1$ year $=3.156\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}$). (a) Calculate Saturn's orbital speed in $\mathrm{m/s}$. [3] (b) State whether this speed is larger or smaller than Earth's orbital speed of about $3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and explain why, in terms of the Sun's gravitational pull. [2] (c) State the direction, relative to Saturn's motion, in which the Sun's gravitational force acts on Saturn. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $T=29.5\times3.156\times10^{7}\approx9.31\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{s}$; $v=\dfrac{2\pi\times1.43\times10^{12}}{9.31\times10^{8}}\approx9.6\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (b) Smaller than Earth's, because Saturn is much farther from the Sun, so the Sun's gravitational pull on it is weaker and a lower orbital speed is enough to maintain a stable orbit. (c) Perpendicular to Saturn's motion, directed from Saturn toward the Sun.
exam_questions.full_solution: Check for (a): $v\times T\approx9.6\times10^{3}\times9.31\times10^{8}\approx8.9\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$, matching $2\pi r\approx8.99\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}$ to within rounding.
mark_scheme: Converts the period into seconds correctly. [1]
Applies $v=2\pi r/T$ correctly. [1]
Reaches a value of approximately $9$-$10\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. [1]
States the speed is smaller than Earth's. [1]
Explains this using weaker gravitational pull at greater distance. [1]
States the force is perpendicular to the motion, directed toward the Sun. [1]
common_errors: Giving the direction of the gravitational force as 'forward, along the orbit' instead of toward the Sun.

challenge_questions.statement: Two planets, A and B, orbit the same star in circular orbits. Planet B's orbital radius is exactly 4 times Planet A's radius, and Planet B's orbital period is exactly 8 times Planet A's period. Without using any specific numbers for radius or period, determine whether Planet B's orbital speed is larger, smaller, or the same as Planet A's, and by what factor.
hints: Write $v=2\pi r/T$ for each planet separately, using a symbol like $r_A$ and $T_A$ for Planet A.
Substitute $r_B=4r_A$ and $T_B=8T_A$ into Planet B's formula.
Form the ratio $v_B/v_A$ and simplify.
challenge_questions.answer: $v_B/v_A=\dfrac{2\pi r_B/T_B}{2\pi r_A/T_A}=\dfrac{r_B}{T_B}\times\dfrac{T_A}{r_A}=\dfrac{4r_A}{8T_A}\times\dfrac{T_A}{r_A}=\dfrac{4}{8}=0.5$. Planet B's orbital speed is half of Planet A's.
challenge_questions.full_solution: This matches the general trend taught in this lesson: Planet B is farther out (larger $r$) and, consistent with weaker gravity at greater distance, it also has the slower orbital speed, even though its period is longer.

mcq.stem: What quantity does a light-year measure?

options.text: Time.
options.why_wrong: confuses the word 'year' inside the unit's name with what the unit actually measures, which is the distance light covers in that time.

options.text: Distance.
Speed.
options.why_wrong: a light-year is a fixed length, not a rate; the speed involved (the speed of light) is used only to define that fixed length.

options.text: Brightness.
options.why_wrong: unrelated; a light-year carries no information about how bright an object appears.

mcq.explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels through vacuum in one year, so it measures distance.

mcq.stem: A planet moves in a stable circular orbit around the Sun. In which direction does the Sun's gravitational force act on the planet?

options.text: Along the direction the planet is moving, pushing it forward.
options.why_wrong: would speed the planet up continuously, which does not happen in a stable circular orbit.

options.text: Directly away from the Sun.
options.why_wrong: would push the planet away rather than bend its path into a closed orbit around the Sun.

options.text: Directly toward the Sun, perpendicular to the planet's velocity.
There is no net gravitational force once the orbit is stable.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes a stable orbit means no force acts; gravity is continuously acting and is exactly what keeps the orbit stable.

mcq.explanation: Gravity acts toward the Sun, perpendicular to the planet's motion, continuously changing its direction without changing its speed; this is what sustains a stable circular orbit.

mcq.stem: How does the Sun mainly release its energy?

options.text: By ordinary chemical combustion, burning hydrogen gas with oxygen.
options.why_wrong: describes chemical burning, which needs oxygen and only rearranges electrons; the Sun's core has no oxygen supply and the process is nuclear, not chemical.

options.text: By radioactive decay of heavy elements in its core.
options.why_wrong: describes a different nuclear process used, for example, to explain some planetary interior heating, not the Sun's main energy source.

options.text: By reflecting light from nearby stars.
options.why_wrong: the Sun is itself the source of the light observed from it, not a reflector of light from elsewhere.

options.text: By nuclear fusion, joining hydrogen nuclei into helium in its core.

mcq.explanation: A stable star like the Sun releases energy through nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, not chemical combustion or radioactive decay.

mcq.stem: Two planets orbit the Sun in circular orbits. Planet X is farther from the Sun than Planet Y. Which statement about their orbital speeds is correct?

options.text: Planet X orbits slower than Planet Y, because the Sun's gravitational pull on it is weaker.
Planet X orbits faster than Planet Y, because it has farther to travel.
options.why_wrong: confuses the longer path length with a higher speed; the Sun's weaker pull at greater distance actually gives a lower orbital speed, not a higher one.

options.text: Both planets must orbit at the same speed, since both are held by the same Sun.
options.why_wrong: ignores that orbital speed depends on distance from the Sun, not just on which star is being orbited.

options.text: Orbital speed cannot be compared without knowing each planet's mass.
options.why_wrong: the orbital speed of a circular orbit, $v=2\pi r/T$, does not require the orbiting planet's own mass at all.

mcq.explanation: Gravitational pull from the Sun weakens with distance, and a weaker pull is matched by a lower orbital speed for a stable circular orbit, so the farther planet (X) orbits more slowly.

mcq.stem: In which regions of the electromagnetic spectrum does the Sun radiate most of its energy?

options.text: Radio and microwave only.
options.why_wrong: the Sun does give out a little radio and microwave radiation, but only a tiny fraction of its output; most of it is at much shorter wavelengths.

options.text: Infrared, visible and ultraviolet.
X-rays and gamma rays only.
options.why_wrong: only a very small part of the Sun's output is X-radiation; the harmful part of ordinary sunlight reaching the ground is ultraviolet, not X-rays or gamma rays.

options.text: Visible light only, since the other regions come from other stars.
options.why_wrong: visible light is only one part of the Sun's output, and every star gives out radiation across a range of the spectrum.

mcq.explanation: The Sun radiates most of its energy in the infrared, visible and ultraviolet regions of the electromagnetic spectrum; this is why it both warms and lights the Solar System.

flashcards.front: What is a light-year?
flashcards.back: The distance light travels through vacuum in one year; it is a unit of distance, not time.

flashcards.front: What is the formula for orbital speed in a circular orbit, and what does each symbol mean?
flashcards.back: $v=2\pi r/T$, where $v$ is orbital speed, $r$ is the orbital radius (a distance) and $T$ is the orbital period (a time).

flashcards.front: Does a planet need a continuous forward push from an engine to keep orbiting?
flashcards.back: No. Gravity acts toward the Sun, perpendicular to the planet's motion, continuously changing direction rather than speed; no extra forward force is needed to sustain a stable orbit.

flashcards.front: How does the Sun's energy release differ from an ordinary fire burning fuel?
flashcards.back: The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion, joining hydrogen nuclei into helium in its core; an ordinary fire releases energy by chemical combustion, which rearranges electrons and requires oxygen. Fusion needs no oxygen, only extreme temperature and pressure.

flashcards.front: Planet A is closer to the Sun than Planet B. Which planet has the higher orbital speed, and why?
flashcards.back: Planet A, because the Sun's gravitational pull is stronger at a smaller distance, requiring a higher orbital speed to maintain a stable circular orbit.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A light-year is a unit of time, not distance.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The word contains 'year', which is normally a time unit, so it is easy to assume the whole phrase measures time.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner answers a distance question in years, or says 'it took 4 light-years' instead of 'it took 4 years to travel 4 light-years'.
misconceptions.correct_model: A light-year is a distance: the distance light travels through vacuum in one year. 'Light-year' names a length, built from a time (one year) and a speed (the speed of light), in the same way '60 mph for one hour' names a distance of 60 miles.
misconceptions.remediation: Always rewrite 'a light-year' as 'the distance light travels in one year' before using it in a calculation, to force the unit back to a length.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A planet needs a continuous forward (tangential) force from an engine or push to keep moving along its orbit.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Everyday moving objects slow down and stop once nothing pushes them, so steady orbital motion feels as if it needs a continuous forward push to sustain it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes gravity as 'pulling the planet along' its orbit, or invents an extra forward force to explain why the planet keeps moving.
misconceptions.correct_model: Gravity acts toward the Sun (centripetal, not forward), continuously changing the planet's direction rather than speeding it up or slowing it down; this continuous change of direction is exactly what keeps the path curving into a closed orbit instead of flying off in a straight line.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw the gravitational force arrow pointing from the planet toward the Sun at several points on the orbit, and show that it is always perpendicular to the direction of travel, never pointing along it.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The Sun is a planet-like object on fire, burning through ordinary chemical combustion.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Fire is the everyday process people know that gives off light and heat, so it is the nearest familiar idea to reach for.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes the Sun as 'burning' its hydrogen the way wood burns, or says it will 'run out of fuel like a fire going out'.
misconceptions.correct_model: The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion, joining hydrogen nuclei together to form helium deep in its core; this is a nuclear process, not ordinary chemical combustion, and it is what keeps a stable star shining for billions of years.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast the two processes directly: chemical burning rearranges electrons between atoms and needs oxygen, while fusion joins nuclei together and needs extreme temperature and pressure, not oxygen.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a light-year as a unit of time.
common_mistakes.why: The word 'year' inside the unit's name is normally a time unit.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Rewrite 'a light-year' as 'the distance light travels in one year' before using it in any calculation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a stable orbit needs a continuous forward engine force to keep the orbiting body moving.
common_mistakes.why: Everyday moving objects need a continuous push to keep going once friction or drag acts on them.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Identify the direction of the gravitational force at several points on the orbit and confirm it always points toward the central body, perpendicular to the motion, never along it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using an orbital period in days or years directly in $v=2\pi r/T$ without converting to seconds.
common_mistakes.why: $r$ is usually already given in metres, so it is easy to forget that $T$ needs the matching SI time unit.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Convert the period into seconds as a separate first step, before substituting into the formula.

exam_notes: State explicitly that a light-year is a distance when asked to define it; do not give only a number without the word 'distance'.
When using $v=2\pi r/T$, show the unit conversion of $T$ into seconds as a separate line, since this is where most marks are lost.
When asked for the direction of the Sun's gravitational force on an orbiting planet, state 'toward the Sun' explicitly, not 'forward' or 'along the orbit'.

summary.big_idea: A light-year turns enormous distances into a usable scale, and the Sun's gravity, acting perpendicular to each planet's motion, bends straight-line paths into stable orbits whose speed decreases the farther out the planet lies.
key_points: A light-year is a distance (the speed of light multiplied by one year), never a time on its own.
Travel time is found with $t=d/c$, exactly the same rearrangement used for any constant-speed problem.
Gravity on an orbiting planet points toward the Sun, perpendicular to its velocity, changing direction rather than speed; no ongoing forward push is needed to sustain a stable orbit.
For a circular orbit, $v=2\pi r/T$; both gravitational field strength and orbital speed decrease as distance from the Sun increases.
A stable star like the Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, not by ordinary chemical combustion.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A light-year measures distance, and a stable circular orbit needs gravity pulling toward the centre, not a forward push, with the pull and the orbital speed both weaker the farther out you go.
